vocabulary.en_definition: A little, a small amount. A beginner uses it constantly, most often to explain how much of the language they have.
Excuse me, used to get someone's attention before you ask them anything. It is the opening move of every question you will ask in the district of Asking the Way.

vocabulary.en: goodbye (said to the one who is leaving)
vocabulary.en_definition: The goodbye said to the person who is leaving. Tibetan has two, and this is the one you use when you are the one staying behind.
vocabulary.thl_note: ཕེབས is the honorific of "to go"; the b is not pronounced — *phe*, not *phebs*.

vocabulary.en: goodbye (said to the one who is staying)
vocabulary.en_definition: The goodbye said to the person who is staying. This is the one you use when you are the one walking out of the door.
vocabulary.thl_note: བཞུགས is *shu* — the b and the final s are both silent. An English reader will want "b-zhugs".

vocabulary.en_definition: Maybe, perhaps. The softener for when yes and no are both too strong — an invitation you have not decided about, a plan that may not happen. It leaves the question open without committing you to anything.
vocabulary.thl_note: *chik chheena* — གཅིག is *chik*, not "g-chig".

vocabulary.en_definition: The polite negative answer, for correcting a wrong guess about you without any sharpness. You will need it the first time someone assumes you are from somewhere you are not.
All right, fine, agreed. The general-purpose word for accepting what has been said or offered.
vocabulary.thl_note: *lakso* — the s of ལགས closes the syllable rather than starting a new one.

vocabulary.en_definition: The word that softens a request. You always meet it inside a whole phrase in this track, so you never have to decide where to put it.
vocabulary.thl_note: *roknhang*. The dictionary's English→Tibetan hits for "please" (མགུ་བ, "to gratify") are the wrong sense entirely.

vocabulary.en_definition: Slowly. It is a word in its own right, and it also sits inside both goodbyes, which is why learning it stops them being two opaque noises.
vocabulary.thl_note: *khaaler*. The ག is unvoiced at the start of a word.

vocabulary.en_definition: Sorry. An apology for something you did or bumped into, rather than a way of getting attention.
vocabulary.thl_note: *gongtak*. The དག prefix is silent; not "d-gongs d-ag".

vocabulary.en_definition: The all-purpose greeting, safe with anyone at any hour of the day. It is the first thing you will say off the bus and the last thing you will stop needing.
Thank you. The words are literally "great kindness", which is why it can sound warmer than the English and is worth using more often, not less.

To ask, in the sense of putting a question to someone. This card is here to be recognised rather than said: the place you actually use the verb is the whole sentence "Can I ask you something?", which you learn in one piece. Seeing the verb alone is only so that you notice it again inside the sentence.

To greet. You meet it inside "Please greet your family for me", which is where it does its work, and the card exists so that the word is familiar when it turns up elsewhere. There is nothing to produce here; recognising it is the whole task.

To talk, to speak. The phrase "Please talk slowly" is where you use it, and that phrase is learned whole. This card asks only for recognition, so that the verb stops being an unidentified sound in the middle of a sentence you already know.
vocabulary.thl_note: *ke chha shepa*, literally "to speak words".

vocabulary.en_definition: Very. It strengthens whatever it is attached to, and it is the difference between the plain thank you and the strengthened one you already know. Learning it late means two fixed courtesies stop being two unrelated noises.
The short, polite way of agreeing with what someone has just said. It is the safe answer: it commits you to nothing beyond agreement.
Afternoon. Useful for arranging when to meet, which is most of what these four words do at this stage.
vocabulary.thl_note: *chhito*. ཕྱ is *ch*, not "ph" followed by "y".

vocabulary.en_definition: Someone's age. Asking it is ordinary politeness here rather than an intrusion, and it comes up early in almost any first conversation.
vocabulary.thl_note: *lo*.

vocabulary.en_definition: Also, too. The small word that adds you or a second thing to what has just been said, as in me too, or that one as well. You will hear it constantly before you need it.
Always, continually. Stronger than every day, and used of things that do not stop.
A boy. Children are the people most likely to talk to a foreigner first, so these words arrive early.
A child, of either sex. The word you use when age matters and sex does not.
vocabulary.thl_note: *thruku*. ཕྲ is a single sound *thra*, not "ph" followed by "r".

vocabulary.en_definition: A country. The answer to where you are from is usually a country, so this word arrives with that question.
The day after tomorrow, in a single word rather than four. English has to build the idea out of parts each time; Tibetan keeps one word for it, and another for the matching day going backwards.
vocabulary.thl_note: *nhangnyin*. The ག is a silent prefix.

vocabulary.en_definition: The day before yesterday, again one word. Between them, the two give you five consecutive days you can name outright, with no counting in the middle.
Evening. The end of the working day and the busiest hour in a teahouse.
vocabulary.thl_note: *gongto*. The ད is a silent prefix.

vocabulary.en_definition: Every day, daily. Said of a habit rather than of a plan.
A few days ago. Vaguer than yesterday and the day before, which is the point of it.
A foreigner, an outsider. This is the word a visitor hears applied to themselves several times a day.
vocabulary.thl_note: *chhigye wa*. ཕྱ is *ch*, not "ph" followed by "y".

vocabulary.en_definition: A friend. It stretches a good deal further than the English word and covers the person you have been drinking tea with for an hour.
vocabulary.thl_note: *throokpo*. གྲ is a voiced *dr*, not "g" followed by "r".

vocabulary.en_definition: The future, time still to come. It is the word for later in general, not for a particular later.
Generally, on the whole. It softens a claim you do not want to make absolutely.
A girl. The pair to boy, and equally likely to be the person addressing you.
The place your family is from, which is not necessarily anywhere you have lived. This, not your current address, is usually what a Tibetan means when they ask where you are from.
vocabulary.thl_note: *phayü*. The final ལ colours the vowel to ü rather than sounding as an l.

vocabulary.en_definition: Last night, yesterday evening. The one arrangement here that is not simply the two obvious words joined, so it is worth hearing on its own.
Later, at some point after this. It is deliberately vague, which is exactly what makes it useful: it lets you leave a conversation without fixing a time to anything.
vocabulary.thl_note: *djela*. རྗ is a single *j*.

vocabulary.en_definition: Lhasa: the city this walk moves through, and the source of the variety of Tibetan taught here.
A man. One of the first words you need to describe someone you have just met to somebody else.
vocabulary.thl_note: *kyepa*. The ས prefix and the final ས are both silent.

vocabulary.en_definition: Marriage, as a thing rather than as something you do. It is here mainly because whether you are married is one of the first questions a stranger will ask you, put without any of the awkwardness an English speaker expects.
Midday, noon. It is a stretch of the day rather than a point on a clock, and it fills the gap between morning and afternoon in the sequence you are learning here.
Midnight. Less immediately useful than the other time words and here to complete them, though it earns its place in District 13, where long-distance buses leave at hours like this one.
Morning. It is a piece of time you can talk about, not a greeting: there is no separate good morning to learn.
vocabulary.thl_note: *shookpa*.

vocabulary.en_definition: A person's name. Asking for someone else's name and offering your own are handled by separate fixed phrases in this district, so you are never asked to pick between them yourself.
vocabulary.thl_note: *ming*.

vocabulary.en_definition: A Nepali person. Worth having early: much of the diaspora passed through Nepal, and in Lhasa the word is heard about traders.
Night. The stretch after everything has closed, rather than a time you arrange to meet in.
vocabulary.thl_note: *tshenmo*. The མ is a silent prefix. Same syllable as མཚན, `name` (H) — a real collision worth telling the learner about once.

vocabulary.en_definition: Now, at this moment. It is one of the most used words in any language and easy to skip past in a wordlist, and it turns up in nearly every arrangement you will hear made.
vocabulary.thl_note: *thaata*. ལྟ is a plain *ta*, and the whole word is heard as two light syllables — not "da l-ta".

vocabulary.en_definition: A person, in the general sense. Useful for counting people in a room or saying who a thing belongs to.
Before, previously, in the past. It points backwards without saying how far.
These days, lately. It frames what is true now against what used to be, and it opens a great many conversations about home.
Tibet: the plateau this whole walk is set on, most of it lying above four thousand metres.
vocabulary.thl_note: *phöö*. The ད is silent and colours the vowel; not "bod".

vocabulary.en_definition: A Tibetan person. You will hear it as a question about yourself more often than you expect, especially if you look as though you might be.
vocabulary.thl_note: *phööpa*. The ད is silent and colours the vowel to ö.

vocabulary.en_definition: To arrive, to reach somewhere. You meet it inside "When did you arrive?", one of the first questions anyone will put to you, and that sentence is learned whole. The card is here so the verb is recognisable when it comes round again on the pilgrimage road.
vocabulary.thl_note: *leppa*. The ས prefix is silent — not "s-leb".

vocabulary.en_definition: To hear. The working form is the phrase "Sorry, I can't hear you well", which is more useful than it sounds in a courtyard with several conversations going on. The verb on its own is for recognition; it is not something to produce.

To introduce, in the sense of presenting one person to another. The sentence you actually use is "Let me introduce my friend", drilled as a single piece; this card asks only that you recognise the verb sitting inside it.
vocabulary.thl_note: *ngotrö shuuwa*. སྤྲ is a single *tr*, not "s-p-r".

vocabulary.en_definition: Today. The first of the three day-words, and the one that turns up in nearly every arrangement you make.
Tomorrow. It closes the district: the last phrase you learn here is see you tomorrow.
Tomorrow evening. Tibetan builds this from tomorrow and evening exactly as English does, so it is two words you already have.
Tonight, the evening of the day you are already in. It is what you need to make a plan that does not require naming a date.
Usually, as a rule. The honest middle between always and sometimes, and the safest of the three for a beginner.
A woman. Pairs with the word for man; both come up constantly in the courtyard conversation this district models.
vocabulary.thl_note: *phüüme*. The ད of བུད is silent and turns the vowel to ü.

vocabulary.en_definition: The counting word for years of a life, as in "twenty years old". It belongs to age specifically, not to years on a calendar.
Yesterday. Completes the set of three, so you can place something before, on, or after the day you are standing in.
